Title: Research on the formation of M1-type alite doped with MgO and SO3—A route to improve the quality of cement clinker with a high content of MgO
Abstract: This paper discusses the effect of SO3 dopants on the M1 polymorph formation and mechanical properties of alite containing a high content of MgO. The structure of the M1 alite is identified by XRD, high-temperature XRD and TEM analysis. A characteristic XRD pattern of M1 alite doped with MgO and SO3 is determined, and TEM results show that M1 alite has an incommensurate modulated structure feature with 2.4 times the subcell dimension along [                                                                                                                  2                                                                                             ¯                                                                                                                           10]H                     ∗ and could be expressed as ha∗ + kb∗ + lc∗ + m/[2.4(−2a∗ + b∗)], where m = ±1. The First-Principles method is used to simulate the structure of M1 alite, and the calculated Delta Cohesive Energy is approximately 11–12 eV between the M1 and M3 alite. Quantitative analysis is performed by the Rietveld method. Mechanical properties results show that appropriate SO3 dopant can improve the compressive strength of alite containing high MgO while over dosed SO3 will lead to a contrary effect because of the decomposition of alite. The relationship between M1% in the alite and the compressive strengths at different ages is also given. The optimal M1% in alite is approximately 68% and the best SO3/MgO ratio is approximately 0.43 because the compressive strength could be maximized at each age.
1_Introduction: 1.1 Background With the rapid development of China, a great deal of cement is required in civil engineering. In 2017, 2.32 × 1010 tons of cement was produced in China. For 33 consecutive years, China has been ranked first in the world in cement production. The industrial research institute predicted that, in 2018, the amount of cement would reach 2.338 × 1010 tons [1].The rapid developments of cement industry certainly induce a series of environmental problems. Two well-known issues associated with the calcination of cement are the energy consumption and air pollution. To decrease environmental problems without reducing the economic value of cement production, technological methods must be introduced to make more sustainable cement. From literature review, it can be seen that non-traditional cements had been developed by some new methods such as, adding ye’elimite to clinker by the secondary heat treatment [2], direct synthesis of alite-ye’elimite clinker (4.8 wt% ye’elimite) [3,4] and activating belite in belite-sulfoaluminate cement [5,6]. However, few studies have been made to improve the quality of cement by controlling the structure of the phase in cement clinker, especially for alite. Alite is one of the most important mineral phases in cement clinker. It is a kind of solid solution of Ca3SiO5 (C3S) with minor oxides. The amount of alite in cement clinker determines the strength of Portland cement. It is known that Ca3SiO5 exhibits seven polymorphs from room temperature (RT) to 1100 °C: three triclinic polymorphs (T1, T2 and T3), three monoclinic polymorphs (M1, M2 and M3) and one rhombohedral polymorph (R) [7–9]. The phase transformations of C3S are given in the following scheme [10]:    pure:    T   1     ↔   620  ° C     T   2     ↔   920  ° C     T   3     ↔   980  ° C     M   1     ↔   990  ° C     M   2     ↔   1070  ° C   R         doped ( mainly Zn or Mg ) :    M   1     ↔   990  ° C     M   2     ↔   1060  ° C     M   3     ↔   1070  ° C   R      M1 and M3 polymorphs are the most stabilized phases in cement clinker. In the past decade, these two polymorphs were investigated widely. The structure of M3 was solved by Nishi [11]. Mumme [12] extracted and solved an alite single-crystal structure from a clinker and identified the < M> unit cell. Unlike the structure of M3 alite, a superstructure for M1 alite has not been determined. Recently, Noirfontaine [10] presented non-averaged models for the M1 polymorph and reported a set of atomic positions. Courtial [13] used five angular windows in X-ray diffraction patterns to identify M1 or M3 polymorphs. Staněk [14] found that the strength of cements with modified M1 was 10% higher than that of cements with modified M3. Furthermore, the alite polymorphs in cement clinkers was also influenced by the amount of MgO and SO3. As the MgO and SO3 are the most common minor components in cement clinkers [15–17], we begin to notice that the structure modification of clinker phase would be another promising way to enhance the performance of cement. Some researchers started focusing on this part. Li [18,19] investigated the effects of SO3 and MgO on both the formation of cement clinker and the polymorphs of alite. Although lots of works regarding the stabilization of M1 alite by doping MgO and SO3, few focused on the relationships between MgO/SO3 and the M1/M3 ratio in alite, moreover, the relationships between the M1/M3 ratio and the compressive strength. Therefore, this paper aims to investigate the relationship between the SO3/MgO ratio and the M1/M3 ratio in alite, as well as the relationship between the M1/M3 ratio in alite and the compressive strength. Some technique methods such as, X-ray powder diffraction (XRD), High-temperature XRD and Transmission electron microscope (TEM) are used to identify M1- and M3-type alite. In this process, the First-Principles method and quantitative analysis by Rietveld method are also adopted.
2_Experiments:
2.1 Sample preparation Bigare [7] mentioned that the limit for a solid solution of MgO in C3S was 2.0 wt% at 1550 °C. This paper focused on a high content of MgO in alite, so 2.0 wt% of MgO was considered for the alite doping. In Ca3SiO5 (C3S), the Mole ratio of CaO and SiO2 was 3:1. When Mg2+ dissolved into C3S structure, the Ca2+ would be substituted by Mg2+ and cause more free lime formation [20]. When S6+ dissolved into C3S structure, the CaO in CaSO4·2H2O also cause more free lime formation [20]. In order to prevent an increasing content of free lime by doping MgO and SO3, the total mole ratio of (CaO + MgO) and SiO2 was 3:1 during the burdening process. That is to say, when calculating the CaO in raw meal, the doped MgO and CaO in CaSO4·2H2O would be taken into consideration. The loadings of the raw meals are given in Table 1 . Alite samples were synthesized using analytical-grade CaCO3, SiO2, MgO and CaSO4·2H2O (XiLong Scientific). The prepared raw meals (1 kg) were homogenized in a ball mill bottle with ethanol and agate balls for 24 h. Then, the liquid meal was dried and pressed into discs (40 g per disc) for the sintering process. Alite samples were sintered in a resistance furnace. Samples were placed in Pt crucibles, heated at a rate of 10 °C/min to calcination temperature at 1000 °C for 30 min, then heated up to sintering temperature (1500 °C) and held for 6 h. The sintered alites were then cooled with liquid nitrogen.
2.2 Characterization XRD analysis was used to characterize the crystalline structure of the alite and identify the transformation of the polymorphs during the heating process. All samples were finely ground to perform the powder diffraction measurements. The XRD patterns of the samples were collected on a Rigaku SmartLab 3000A diffractometer (Japan) with a Cu Kα radiation source (wavelength = 0.154 nm). The accelerating voltage, accelerating current, and step size of the tests were 40 kV, 20 mA, and 0.02°, respectively. The patterns were collected over a scanning range of 10 - 70° at a speed of 0.5° per minute. High-temperature XRD analysis was performed by a Rigaku SmartLab TM 9 kV diffractometer (Japan) with a Cu Kα radiation source (wavelength = 0.154 nm and without K α2), in which the accelerating voltage, accelerating current, and step size of the tests were 45 kV, 200 mA, and 0.02°, respectively. High-temperature XRD patterns were collected over a scanning range of 10–70° at a speed of 10° per min at each temperature. The heating process was performed at a speed of 10 °C/min. The patterns were collected every 20 °C after the temperature reached 500 °C. The temperature would hold during the XRD data collection Images of the SAED patterns were recorded using TEM (Model JEM-2100UHR, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The device was equipped with a double-tilt goniometer, where the maximum tilting angle was ±20° around both the x- and y-axes. The Mumme’s [12] average model (Space group: Cm; a = 1.222 nm, b = 0.708 nm, c = 0.930 nm, α = 90°, β = 114.93°, γ = 90°, Ca18Si6O30, named as pure M3 C3S) have been exported as the initial crystal structure to do the geometry optimization by the first principles calculations which has been performed by CASTEP code [21] based on the density functional theory (DFT [22,23]). Furthermore, different dosages of MgO and SO3 substituted into the above mentioned optimized M3 crystal structures are also investigated by the first principles calculations. Considering the limit of solid solution of MgO and SO3, one S6+ substituted for a Si4+ and Ca2+ (in order to guarantee the conservation of charge, a Ca2+ would be taken away from the structure) and (S6+ + Mg2+) co-substituted Si4+ and Ca2+ were discussed. After substitution, the structural formulae were Ca17Si5SO30 (the content of S6+ was 2.33%) and Ca16MgSi5SO30 (the content of S6+ was 2.36% and the content of Mg2+ was 1.77%). The geometry optimization parameters in CASTEP are demonstrated that the core electrons are treated with the ultrasoft pseudo potential method. The exchange-correlation effects of the valence electrons were described by the generalized gradient approximation (GGA [24]) parameterized by Perdew - Burke - Ernzrhof (PBE [25]) function. The Brillouin zone was sampled with 1 × 2 × 2 k-points using the Monkhorst and Pack method [26] respectively. The energy minimization and action of atomic forces algorithm was the Broyden – Fletcher – Goldfarb - Shanno (BFGS) method [27,28]. An energy cutoff of 340 eV was used for expanding the Kohn-Sham wave functions. The energy convergence criteria were set as follows: the force on the atoms were set to 0.03 eV/Å, the stress on each atom was set to 0.05 GPa, the atomic displacement was less than 0.001 Å and the energy change per atom was set to be less than 1.0e−6 eV. The Cohesive Energy was also calculated and the main steps were followed by Wang [29]. The Rietveld quantitative analysis was performed and the structures used for refinements were: M1 C3S [10], M3 C3S ICSD, No. 64759 [11], β-C2S, ICSD, No. 81096, γ-C2S, ICSD, No. 81095, f-CaO, ICSD, No. 52783 [30], MgO, ICSD, No. 31051 [31], CaSO4, ICSD, No. 1956 [32]. Compressive strength measurements were performed by an AEC-201-type automatic cement strength tester (Wuxi, China). The constant loading rate during compression was 2400 N/s. The specific surface areas of all samples were controlled at 300 ± 20 m2/kg with a 0.26 water/cement ratio (w/c). Cubic paste samples (20 × 20 × 20 mm) were cured at 20 ± 1 °C and 95% relative humidity (RH). Then, the samples were removed from the mould after 1 d and immersed in water at 20 °C until they were utilized for compressive strength testing.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 M1-type alite identification  3.1.1 XRD analysis at room temperature An exhaustive investigation of the polymorphs of alite was performed using XRD techniques, and the results are illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2  . Li [18] had reported nine characteristic windows in the XRD patterns that can be used to distinguish M1 alite from M3 alite in cement clinker. Here, six of the nine windows in Li’s article were chosen to distinguish between the M1 alite and M3 alite after doping with MgO and SO3. Compared the windows W2, W4, W5 and W6 in Fig. 2 with the same area mentioned in reference [18] (Especially the peak between 36.5° and 37° in W5, M3 alite had the characteristic peak at about 36.7° while this peak was not appeared in M1 alite), Blank, 0.5%, and 1.0% SO3 samples were identified as M3 alite. The peak at approximately 25.5° in W1 and two peaks in W2 were only observed in M1 that was obtained after doping with both MgO and SO3 [18]. So, 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3 samples were determined to produce M1 alite. Meanwhile, W4 and W6 show the fingerprint areas of C3S [7,9]. Taylor [15] had reported the XRD patterns of the fingerprint regions for C3S with different modifications. By comparing the obtained patterns with the fingerprint regions in reference [15], Blank, 0.5%, and 1.0% SO3 samples corresponded to M3 alite, while 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3 samples corresponded to M1, as mentioned before.   3.1.2 High-temperature XRD analysis To investigate the fingerprint regions of M1 C3S at high temperature, a pure C3S sample was heated from room temperature (RT) to 1100 °C. The test methods and instrument used are given in the Characterization section. The fingerprint regions at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 3 , and the XRD pattern at 980 °C is shown in Fig. 4 . From Fig. 3, we could determine that the polymorphs of pure C3S at room temperature were T1 and T2 at 620 °C, T3 at 900 °C, M1 at 960 °C, M2 at 1000 °C and R at 1100 °C, which match results previously reported by Bigare [7]. During the heating process, the polymorph of M3 was not found in the XRD patterns, which corresponded with Noirfontaine [10].  Fig. 4 shows the XRD pattern of pure C3S at 980 °C, and an M1-type polymorph could be identified from the fingerprint area. This pattern was the same as the patterns of samples doped with 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3, which confirmed the polymorphs of them (samples doped with 1.5%, 2.0% and 2.5% SO3) were M1 on the other side.   3.1.3 TEM To further resolve the M1-type and M3-type alite at the microscale, the 1.0% SO3 sample and the 1.5% SO3 sample were examined by TEM. The fingerprint area of the XRD patterns from Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were given in Fig. 8  and it was found that the fingerprint area was similar to the 1.5% SO3 sample, which was given in Fig. 2 (W4 and W6). Notably, the TEM showed that alite with this kind of fingerprints tended to be M1-type. According to the structural simulation using First-Principles Calculations, doping with MgO and SO3 could change the M3-type alite to an M1-type. The calculated energies of pure M3 C3S, Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 are shown in Table 2 . The Delta Cohesive Energies of Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were similar, and over 10 eV higher than pure M3 C3S which indicated that the polymorphs of Ca17Si5SO30 and Ca16MgSi5SO30 were different from pure M3 C3S. This result is consistent with the previously discussed results from the simulated XRD.
3.2 Quantitative analysis Li [19] reported the correlation between SO3/MgO and C3S composition in cement clinker, but the correlation between SO3/MgO and the composition of M1 type alite was not mentioned. During the formation of alite doped with MgO and SO3, part of the S6+ was volatilized and part of the S6+ was doped into C3S. This would lead to an inhomogeneous distribution of S6+ in the resultant alite. M1-type and M3-type alite would also be coexistent. To correlate the SO3/MgO to the composition of the M1-type alite, quantitative analyses of the samples were calculated by the Rietveld method. Several examples of Rietveld refinements are shown in Fig. 9 , and the complete results are given in Table. 3 .  Fig. 10  shows the variations in the phase composition with increasing SO3/MgO. The increasing content of SO3 promoted the formation of M1-type alite and the transformation of γ-C2S into β-C2S. The content of C3S, C2S and f-CaO depended on the dosage of SO3. Low dosages of SO3 accelerated the reaction of C2S and CaO to form C3S, while excessive amounts of SO3 caused the decomposition of C3S. An optimal content of SO3 that could provide a maximized C3S content could certainly be determined. Nonlinear fittings were used to analyse the results. The equations used for the fitting are given in Fig. 11 , and the modelled results were in good agreement with the experimental data.
3.3 Compressive strength Because the compressive strength is an important index that reflects the properties of fresh and hardened cement pastes, the influence of the SO3 in alite with a high content of MgO on the compressive strengths at different ages is further investigated, as shown in Fig. 12 . When the SO3 was below a certain value, the compressive strengths at different ages increased with increasing SO3. However, when the SO3 exceeded that value, the compressive strengths decreased with increased SO3. This could be explained by the decomposition of C3S. Combined with the content of C3S, when the samples had a similar content of C3S (such as the 2.0% SO3 sample and the 1.0% SO3 sample, see Table. 3), the one with the larger content of M1 alite would have a greater compressive strength. Furthermore, the corresponding increase in ratios as listed in Fig. 12, a similar trend in the development of compressive strength can be clearly observed. However, the increase in the ratio decreases with the curing age. For the sample with 1.5% SO3, the ratio increases to as high as 36.0% after 1 d of curing, while the increased ratio decreases back down to 9.5% after 28 d. These results indicate that the effect of SO3 addition on the early development of strength is significant. To help predict the compressive strength of the clinker at a later time, a relationship between M1% in alite, SO3/MgO and compressive strength was established. Nonlinear fitting was used to simulate the curve, and it was found that a cubic polynomial (y = a + bX + cX2 + dX3) perfectly fit the curve. The fitting information is given in Figs. 13  and Fig. 14 . The optimal M1% in alite was approximately 68% and the best SO3/MgO ratio was approximately 0.43 because the compressive strength could be maximized at each age.
4_Conclusions:
The results show that in low doses, SO3 promotes the formation of alite. If overdosed, however, SO3 will lead to the decomposition of alite, which is the primary factor for the decreased compressive strength of alite with a high SO3 content.
The TEM results show that M1 alite has an incommensurate modulated structure feature with 2.4 times the subcell dimension along [    2   ¯     10]H ∗ and could be expressed as ha∗ + kb∗ + lc∗ + m/[2.4(−2a∗ + b∗)], where m = ±1. The characteristic XRD patterns (fingerprint region) of alite doped with MgO and SO3 were determined by X-ray powder diffraction at both room temperature and high temperature. The simulated structure of M1 alite was calculated using the First-Principles method and the Delta Cohesive Energy between M1 and M3 alite is approximately 11–12 eV.
The M1% in alite increases with the increase of SO3 and has a strong linear relationship with the ratio of SO3/MgO, which can be defined by the equation:     M 1 -   C   3   S %   M 1 -   C   3   S % + M 3 -   C   3   S %   × 100 %   = 24.73 + 108.11 ∗ SO3/MgO (%). The relationship between M1% in alite and the compressive strength can be fit with a cubic polynomial equation. According to the fitting results, optimal M1% in alite was approximately 68% and the best SO3/MgO ratio was approximately 0.43 because the compressive strength could be maximized at each age.
